content: Advanced Emergency Medical Technician Critical Care (EMT-CC) is a specialized Emergency Medical Services (EMS) certification that is unique to the state of New York. The training curriculum for EMT-CCs is more advanced than the national standard for EMT-Intermediate (EMT-I/99). EMT-CCs are classified as Advanced Life Support (ALS) providers in New York and are trained to perform advanced airway management, administer intravenous fluids, monitor and defibrillate cardiac rhythms, and use or administer medications for both adult and pediatric patients. To become an EMT-CC, candidates must first hold a current EMT-Basic certification. Most instructors also require candidates to have at least one year of active experience as an EMT-Basic. The training program typically involves 300-400 hours of total instruction, which is divided into 175-225 hours of classroom and practical laboratory work, 50-75 hours of clinical experience, and 75-100 hours of field internship. At the conclusion of the program, students must pass both a state practical skills exam and a written exam to achieve certification. However, maintaining certification requires ongoing continuing medical education, as the learning process for an EMT-CC is continuous. Classroom Training The classroom portion of the EMT-CC program covers a wide range of topics, including: The foundational principles of the EMT-Critical Care Technician role. An overview of human anatomy and physiology, as well as the roles and responsibilities of an EMT-CC. Emergency pharmacology, including the administration of medications and establishing venous access. Advanced airway management and ventilation techniques. Comprehensive patient assessment, including history taking, physical examination techniques, clinical decision-making, and effective communication and documentation. The curriculum also includes training in managing trauma emergencies, such as: Understanding trauma systems and mechanisms of injury. Managing hemorrhage and shock. Treating burns, as well as head, thoracic, and abdominal trauma. Hands-on trauma practical laboratory sessions. Additionally, the program addresses a variety of medical emergencies, including: Respiratory and cardiovascular emergencies. Diabetic emergencies and allergic reactions. Poisonings and overdoses. Neurological emergencies and non-traumatic abdominal emergencies. Environmental, behavioral, gynecological, and obstetrical emergencies. Neonatal resuscitation, as well as care for pediatric and geriatric patients. Clinical Training During the clinical phase, students spend significant time observing and working alongside healthcare professionals in various hospital settings. These settings may include the Emergency Department, Operating Room, Coronary Care Unit, Pediatric Intensive Care Unit, Neonatal Intensive Care Unit, Burn Unit, and Medical Intensive Care Unit. The goal of this phase is to expose students to a diverse range of patients and medical conditions, allowing them to practice and refine their clinical skills and knowledge in a supervised, educational environment. Field Training In the field training phase, EMT-CC students participate in real-world EMS calls that require ALS-level skills. These calls are conducted under the supervision of an EMT-CC or Paramedic preceptor. This phase allows students to apply the cognitive knowledge and technical skills they have developed during classroom and clinical training to actual pre-hospital care scenarios. Scope of Practice EMT-CCs operate under a set of medical protocols that are overseen by a medical director. These protocols are typically presented in an algorithmic format and include both standing orders and orders that require direct communication with medical control via radio or telephone. Compared to Paramedics, EMT-CCs have fewer standing orders and require more frequent contact with medical control. However, all ALS protocols adhere to current guidelines for Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS), Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS), Pre-hospital Trauma Life Support (PHTLS), Basic Trauma Life Support (BTLS), and Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS). EMT-CCs are trained and authorized to perform a variety of advanced medical procedures, including: Establishing venous access and administering medications. Performing endotracheal intubation and advanced airway management. Interpreting electrocardiograms (ECGs) and performing electrical cardiac therapies. Conducting chest decompression and intraosseous access. Adhering to all state-defined Basic Life Support (BLS) protocols. This comprehensive training and scope of practice enable EMT-CCs to provide critical care in pre-hospital settings, ensuring high-quality emergency medical services for patients in need.
